title: Chinese bikes are not "cheap" anymore! Evolve Cima Long Term Review.

takeaways.text: Geometry is unusually Western for a Chinese frame: about 10–12 mm more stack than an equivalent Giant TCR, close to a Tarmac SL8/SL9, with a steep seat angle and a steep head angle that shortens trail.
With size 47–48 shoes and rearward cleats he gets drive-side heel rub where the chainstay flares around the UDH hardware.

Rear brake mounts are faced bare of paint, so use an anodised adapter to avoid corrosion; the BSA shell is bonded in two halves and well faced, and the bottom bracket still spun freely after winter riding.
The Kreuza integrated bar is well made but fits only 1 1/8 in steerers; the fork steerer is very thick with a glass-fibre inner layer, and the expander plug holds preload well.

Fault: the seatpost Di2 battery clamp lost grip every three to four months and dropped the battery into the frame, once forcing bottom-bracket removal; other owners told him the same, and tape now holds it.
Read the manual before removing the front-derailleur mount: its nut plate falls inside the frame unless held with an old cable, and fishing it out took him about 45 minutes.
He runs a 32 mm rear tire with plenty of room either side (rim width not stated).
He rates the stiffness-to-weight balance close to a Tarmac or TCR and more comfortable than a TCR on broken roads, but warns that service given to reviewers may differ from what customers receive.

disclosure: Evolve sent the frame free of charge; the presenter says the video is not paid, and the description includes a Panda Podium referral link.
summary: Final review after ten months as the presenter's main road bike: geometry, hardware details, a recurring Di2 battery-holder fault and ride quality.
